subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Elizabeth found out on a bus ride back from the town market. Her brother Yash, who everyone thought was still working at the tile shop, had lost the job in spring and taken a loan from a local lender to keep up the pretence. Now the lender's man had begun calling at the house. Their parents thought the calls were for the shop. That evening, at the tea stall near the bus stand, she told only Aunt Mala, the retired schoolteacher, who listened without gasping. Later Elizabeth sat down with Yash. “I won't say it behind your back,” she said. “But they need to hear it before the man comes again. You tell them, and I sit beside you.”

qa.q: What had Yash lost in spring?
qa.a: Yash had lost the job at the tile shop in spring.

qa.q: What did Elizabeth worry about and want when deciding who should know?
qa.a: Elizabeth was weighing Yash's privacy against the parents' right to know before the lender's man came again. She also did not want to use the secret against him.

qa.q: What choice did Elizabeth make about telling the parents?
qa.a: She asked Yash to tell them himself and offered to sit beside him, instead of speaking behind his back.

qa.q: How might Yash feel when Elizabeth says, “I sit beside you”?
qa.a: Yash may feel relieved that he is not left alone with it, though probably still ashamed, since he had kept up the pretence for months.

grounding: An adult who learns a hard family truth weighs privacy against safety, asks a trusted person for support and does not use the secret as a weapon.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Selin had read the letter twice before she folded it back into her late grandmother's box. It said her mother had given a baby up for adoption years before Selin was born. Nobody had ever spoken of it. That night in the flat above the bakery, Selin's father was watching a match, and her mother was on the phone with a cousin. Selin did not say a word. On Sunday she met Abebe, an old family friend who had known her mother since school, at the park. “Part of me wants to tell Papa tonight,” Selin said. “But it's her story. Maybe she should first hear from me that I know.” Abebe nodded. “Who else knows is hers to decide. Ask her gently, alone, and don't carry it as a weapon.” Selin nodded slowly.

qa.q: What did the letter in Selin's grandmother's box say?
qa.a: It said her mother had given a baby up for adoption years before Selin was born.

qa.q: What was Selin feeling when she stayed silent that night in the flat?
qa.a: Selin was probably shaken and protective of her mother, so she kept the letter to herself until she could think it through.

qa.q: What could Selin do next after the talk with Abebe?
qa.a: Selin could ask her mother gently, when they are alone, and let her mother decide who else should know.

qa.q: How might Selin's mother feel if she found out that Selin knew?
qa.a: Selin's mother might feel exposed and worried at first, so speaking gently and privately, not in front of the family, would matter to her.

grounding: An adult who learns a hard family truth weighs privacy and fairness, seeks a trusted person's advice and decides not to use the secret as a weapon.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: In the hospital waiting room, Tanuja's aunts were arguing about who should sign the forms. Tanuja had just come back from the records desk, where a clerk asked whether 'the other son, Mr Deepak' should be informed too. Her father had no son. Or so she had thought. The aunts' voices rose. Mausi snapped that Tanuja's father had always been careless with family. Tanuja felt the words sitting on her tongue, a way to win the argument in one sentence. She kept quiet. At lunch she found Ishita, the hospital counsellor she knew from college. 'I don't know if it's mine to tell,' Tanuja said. 'Or if Papa should, when he's well.' Ishita asked, 'Who needs to know now, for his care, and who can wait?' That evening Tanuja told only her mother, gently, and they decided to ask Papa together once he was out of danger.

qa.q: Who did the clerk ask about at the records desk?
qa.a: 'The other son, Mr Deepak', whom Tanuja had not known about.

qa.q: What was Tanuja tempted to do during the aunts' argument, and why did she hold back?
qa.a: She felt an angry pull to win the argument by revealing the secret, but held back, unsure it was hers to tell.

qa.q: How did Ishita's question help Tanuja decide?
qa.a: It split the problem into who needs to know now for Papa's care and who can wait, so Tanuja told only her mother.

qa.q: How might Tanuja's mother experience that evening conversation?
qa.a: She hears hard news gently and in private, and is included in deciding how to raise it with Papa, rather than hearing it in a family fight.

grounding: An adult who stumbles on a hard family truth seeks support, weighs who needs to know and does not use it as a weapon.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage:
Hrithik,
You're the only one I can tell. Last week I found out why my cousin Leena is always so tired. She's sixteen, and she's been washing dishes at a restaurant till midnight, because her father, Uncle Thomas, lost his job in March and hasn't told anyone.
At Sunday lunch, Uncle Thomas was boasting about buying a new car, and my brother joked about 'rich relatives'. I could have said it right there. Part of me wanted to, just to shut him up. I didn't.
That same evening I went to Aunty Sheela, Leena's mother, alone, and told her what I'd seen. She cried, then phoned Leena and brought her home. Now we're quietly helping Uncle Thomas look for work.
I'm not telling the rest of the family. It's his story. But I needed to tell someone. Can we talk tonight?
Jomon

qa.q: How old is Leena?
qa.a: She's sixteen.

qa.q: Why did Jomon feel the urge to reveal the secret at Sunday lunch?
qa.a: Jomon felt irritated by Uncle Thomas's boasting and was tempted to use the secret to shut him up, but held back.

qa.q: Which step did Jomon take that protected Leena, and why was it wise?
qa.a: Going to Aunty Sheela alone that same evening; it got Leena home quickly without shaming Uncle Thomas in front of everyone.

qa.q: How might Uncle Thomas feel if the secret had come out at Sunday lunch?
qa.a: He would likely have felt humiliated and exposed in front of the whole family, making it harder to accept help.

grounding: An adult weighs safety, privacy and fairness in handling a family secret, tells only the person who can act, and seeks a friend's support.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: Ramesh, can I tell you something, as a friend? Rafiq's big headache this month. Abbu called me alone last week. He has a heart condition, and he wants to go for surgery without telling my brother or my sisters. 'They'll panic,' he said. So I've been carrying it. Then on Friday my brother shouted at me in front of everyone for not visiting enough, and I nearly said, 'You don't even know Abbu is sick.' I stopped myself. It would have been a weapon, not the truth told properly. I think my sisters have a right to know before the surgery, but it's Abbu's news to give. So tomorrow I'm going to sit with him and ask him to tell them himself, with me right there. Does that sound fair to you?

qa.q: What does Abbu want to do without telling the others?
qa.a: Go for surgery without telling Rafiq's brother or sisters.

qa.q: What was Rafiq feeling when the brother shouted in front of everyone?
qa.a: Rafiq felt angry and hurt, tempted to use the secret as a weapon, but stopped.

qa.q: What is wise about Rafiq's plan for tomorrow?
qa.a: It respects that the news is Abbu's to give while being fair to the siblings, by asking Abbu to tell them himself with Rafiq there for support.

qa.q: How might Rafiq's sisters feel if they learned about the surgery only afterwards?
qa.a: They would likely feel shut out and hurt, having had no chance to support Abbu before it.

grounding: An adult holding a parent's hard secret weighs fairness and privacy, confides in a friend and refuses to use it as a weapon.

subtopic: Family systems (joint family, in-laws, favourite child, family roles and secrets)
passage: I'm Arohi's cousin, so I only saw pieces of it. At Nani's eightieth birthday, Arohi was quiet all evening, an old envelope in her lap. Later I heard Kishore, her younger brother, tease her about something small, and Arohi's jaw tightened. For a second I thought she would snap back with whatever was in that envelope. She didn't. She slipped it into her bag and went up to the terrace with Masi for almost an hour. From the stairs I could see Masi listening, nodding, once holding Arohi's hand. The next week Arohi told me only this: "It's something about Papa's past. Mummy, Papa and I will decide who hears it. Not a birthday party." I still don't know what the envelope held. I know she chose not to throw it.

qa.q: What was Arohi holding in her lap at Nani's birthday?
qa.a: Arohi had an old envelope in her lap.

qa.q: What does Arohi's tightened jaw suggest she was feeling when Kishore teased her?
qa.a: She was hurt and angry, and tempted for a moment to hit back with what she knew, but she held it in.

qa.q: Which of Arohi's choices worked, and why?
qa.a: She took the news to Masi, someone she trusted, and planned to decide with her parents who should hear it, instead of using it to win a small fight.

qa.q: What would change if Arohi had used the envelope against Kishore that evening?
qa.a: Kishore and the whole family would have learnt a painful truth in public at a party, hurting Papa's privacy and turning the secret into a weapon.

grounding: The narrator watches Arohi keep a hard family truth private, seek support from Masi, and refuse to use it as a weapon.
